evidence_quote: Each charter school collects applications and holds its own lottery in years the school is over-subscribed. Siblings of students already attending the school are guaranteed a seat, as are students continuing on from earlier grades. Students can apply to as many charter schools as they like
resolved_title: Accountability and Flexibility in Public Schools: Evidence from Boston's Charters and Pilots (NBER WP 15549)
notes: Lottery sample of applicants to over-subscribed Boston charter and pilot schools; no achievement or demographic rule. Kraft rows 1 (K-12, n 11000) and 19 (grades 4-8, n 9141) both point to this paper; row 19 is labeled Angrist et al. 2011 in Kraft but its author list starts with Abdulkadiroglu, so treated as a twin (likely the middle school subsample). Text is the NBER working paper version of the 2011 QJE article.

evidence_quote: Each charter school collects applications and holds its own lottery in years the school is over-subscribed. Siblings of students already attending the school are guaranteed a seat, as are students continuing on from earlier grades. Students can apply to as many charter schools as they like
resolved_title: Accountability and Flexibility in Public Schools: Evidence from Boston's Charters and Pilots (NBER WP 15549)
notes: Twin of row 1 (same paper, same codes). Kraft citation reads Angrist et al. 2011 but Kraft author list begins Abdulkadiroglu, Angrist, Dynarski, Kane, matching the QJE article; grades 4-8 and n 9141 suggest the middle school lottery subsample. Lottery applicants to over-subscribed charter and pilot schools; no eligibility rule beyond applying.

evidence_quote: We conducted the study in three large urban school districts, one in the northeast, one in the midwest, and one in the south, each of which had a superintendent or technology director interested in evaluating the CAI program already in use in their district.
resolved_title: Technology's Edge: The Educational Benefits of Computer-Aided Instruction (NBER WP 14240)
notes: Pre-algebra and algebra classes in participating schools were randomly assigned to computer lab or traditional instruction (p. 16); no student rule. Districts volunteered (tie-breaker 6). Districts are high-minority but not selected on that. Post-test sample 1,873 students, so Kraft n 3451 may reflect a larger baseline roster; not confirmed in text. Quote has the paper's en dashes replaced with commas.

evidence_quote: In each year, half of all students in grades three through six became eligible for the financial incentive which can be as much as $100 per student.
resolved_title: Paying to Learn: The Effect of Financial Incentives on Elementary School Test Scores (NBER WP 16333)
notes: Randomization by grade-within-school across all four Coshocton, Ohio elementary schools; all students in grades 3 to 6 were in the sample. Poor Appalachian district but not selected on that trait. Text is the 2010 NBER version of the 2012 REStat article.

evidence_quote: The target population for this study is comprised of students in second through fifth grades who are below grade level in reading or math, but not by more than two years. At the beginning of the study, local staff members (that is, the district coordinator and teachers) were asked to identify students in need of supplemental academic support
resolved_title: The Evaluation of Enhanced Academic Instruction in After-School Programs: Final Report (NCEE 2009-4077)
notes: Students identified by local staff as below grade level, drawn from the pool signing up for the existing after-school program, then randomly assigned (opt_in 1). Sites also chosen purposefully to serve this target population. Kraft effects (-0.04 reading, 0.09 math) are from the second-year 27-center sample; Kraft n 1218 not verified against the report.

evidence_quote: This study targeted middle schools in districts in Southern California in which English language learner students classified as limited English proficient comprised at least 10 percent of the student population.
resolved_title: Evaluation of Quality Teaching for English Learners (QTEL) Professional Development: Final Report (NCEE 2012-4005)
notes: School-level RCT; schools chosen for EL concentration (10 percent LEP cutoff), a non-achievement school trait. Outcome sample is all grade 8 students of ELA and ELD teachers in 52 schools, not only ELs. Report Year 3 grade 8 sample is 9,555 intervention plus 8,625 control; Kraft n 8720 does not match that total, may be a single year or group.

evidence_quote: To qualify for the study, schools had to meet requirements under Title I (schoolwide or targeted) or Missouri's historical requirements for Title II.D (50 percent of students in poverty) and be part of the Small Rural School Achievement program or the Rural and Low-Income School program
resolved_title: The Impact of eMINTS Professional Development on Teacher Instruction and Student Achievement: Year 1 Report (AIR, January 2013)
notes: High-poverty rural Missouri middle schools, grades 7 and 8; all students of participating teachers. Report states 3,610 students, matching Kraft n. WWC row for this study is the Meyers et al. 2016 journal version of the same trial and agrees (rural, Title I or majority FRPL).

evidence_quote: This 3-year randomized control study found that over time coaches positively affected student achievement in grades 3, 4, and 5.
resolved_title: The Impact of Elementary Mathematics Coaches on Student Achievement (Elementary School Journal, 2011)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (ERIC EJ963689, DOI 10.1086/657654) is the correct article, Campbell and Malkus 2011, but it describes only the design (coaches placed in randomized schools, grades 3 to 5) and states no rule for how schools or students were chosen. No open full text was found. Kraft's n 24,759 is consistent with a whole-school sample but the abstract does not say so, so unclear rather than universal.

evidence_quote: The sample population was restricted to grades two through five, since students in these grades typically are assigned a single instructor for all subjects.
resolved_title: National Board Certification and Teacher Effectiveness: Evidence from a Random Assignment Experiment (NBER WP 14608)
notes: LAUSD schools with an NBPTS applicant teacher; principals volunteered (p. 14) and students were randomly assigned between the applicant and a comparison teacher. No student rule. WWC row reports no sample characteristics.

evidence_quote: Eligible schools were those with sets of TFA and comparison teachers teaching math classes that could form a randomization block for the study. Math courses eligible for inclusion included 6th, 7th, and 8th grade math; general high school math; Algebra I; Algebra II; and Geometry.
resolved_title: Supplying Disadvantaged Schools with Effective Teachers: Experimental Evidence on Secondary Math Teachers from Teach For America (Chiang, Clark, and McConnell journal version)
notes: Text is the journal article by the same team, not the Clark et al. 2013 NCEE report, but it describes the same trial. Districts chosen for concentrations of TFA math teachers; schools are high-poverty because TFA places there, not by a study rule (tie-breaker 6). Article reports 5,790 students randomized with TFA teachers; Kraft n 12699 likely pools the TFA and Teaching Fellows arms of the NCEE report, unverified here.

evidence_quote: Schools that had recently hired alternatively certified (AC) teachers were recruited to participate in the study. If the AC teacher was teaching the same grade level as a relative novice traditionally certified (TC) teacher, the school was eligible to participate in the evaluation.
evidence_location: p. 18 (PDF page; executive summary p. xvii)
resolved_title: An Evaluation of Teachers Trained Through Different Routes to Certification: Final Report (NCEE 2009-4043)
notes: Students in study grades randomly assigned between AC and TC teachers; no student rule. Report states 2,600 students in 63 schools, close to Kraft n 2610.

evidence_quote: The eligible population consists of the 22,314 students who were enrolled in the 23 county middle schools when the early-seventh-grade questionnaire was distributed. The longitudinal sample comprises those students whose parents gave active consent for them to take part in the study
resolved_title: Comer's School Development Program in Prince George's County, Maryland: A Theory-Based Evaluation (AERJ 1999)
notes: All 23 district middle schools randomized by matched pairs; all enrolled students eligible, with 12,398 in the longitudinal sample after parental consent for surveys and exclusion of Latino students, matching Kraft n 12000. County chosen for its predominantly African American population but the sample is every student, so universal. Quote fixes the OCR spacing in who.

evidence_quote: Generally, youths, age 14 to 15, are initially assessed on their reading and math skills by an emancipation preparation advisor using The Community College Foundation (TCCF)-devised assessments. These assessments produce grade-level equivalent scores. Those who are assessed as being one to three years behind their school grade level in either reading or math are referred to TCCF for tutoring.
resolved_title: Evaluation of the Early Start to Emancipation Preparation-Tutoring Program, Los Angeles County, California: Final Report (Multi-Site Evaluation of Foster Youth Programs, July 2008)
notes: Foster youth (a non-achievement trait) screened for being one to three years behind grade level, so tie-breaker 1 gives targeted_low. Referred youths were randomly assigned; no application. Analysis sample 445 versus Kraft n 402. The wwc-codes.csv row for study 202 holds the Bifulco et al. 2009 magnet school text, which is the wrong study.

evidence_quote: Many CPS schools use lotteries to allocate spots when oversubscribed. In this paper, we use lottery data from 194 separate lotteries at 19 high schools.
resolved_title: The Effect of School Choice on Student Outcomes: Evidence from Randomized Lotteries (NBER WP 10113, 2003 version of the 2006 Econometrica article)
notes: Sample is eighth-grade applicants to oversubscribed Chicago public high school lotteries (p. 9); no achievement or demographic rule. Text file is the earlier NBER working paper, not the published version, same study.

evidence_quote: Any student who reported not having a home computer was eligible for the study.
resolved_title: Experimental Evidence on the Effects of Home Computers on Academic Achievement among Schoolchildren (NBER version)
notes: Eligibility was lack of a home computer, identified by an in-class survey of all students in 15 Central Valley schools; a program rule that is not achievement-based. Schools are poorer than the California average but no poverty criterion for choosing them is stated. Sample of 1,123 students matches Kraft n.

evidence_quote: Schools that signed up to participate serve as the basis for our randomization. All randomization was done at the school level.
resolved_title: Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials (NBER working paper version of the 2011 QJE article)
notes: Four school-level experiments (Dallas grade 2, New York grades 4 and 7, Washington DC grades 6 to 8, Chicago grade 9); Kraft grade list 2,4,7,9 omits DC. Schools volunteered (tie-breaker 6); Chicago used the 40 smallest of 70 volunteers, described as low-performing but not chosen by an achievement rule. Students needed parental consent to receive payments, but the analysis is intent-to-treat on all students in study schools, so opt_in 0. Kraft n 27000 approximates the pooled sample.

evidence_quote: Three hundred and ninety-six high-poverty schools were included in the random assignment process: 187 elementary schools, 82 middle schools, 39 K-8 schools, 73 high schools, one K-12 school, and 14 schools serving middle and high school students.
evidence_location: p. 3 (WWC single study review, Appendix A, Study sample)
resolved_title: WWC Review of the Report: Teacher Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from New York City Public Schools (WWC Single Study Review, September 2013)
notes: The text file is the eight-page WWC review of Fryer's paper, not the paper itself, so the code rests on a WWC summary. The bonus program operated in high-need schools chosen by the district; all students in those schools are in the analysis. Kraft n 185612 fits a 396-school sample. Twin candidate: study 301 is a different Fryer paper (Houston).

evidence_quote: Twenty-four third-, fourth-, and fifth-grade teachers and their classrooms participated in the study.
evidence_location: p. 1 (ERIC abstract) and p. 7 (volunteer teacher sample)
resolved_title: A Study of Cooperative Learning in Mathematics, Writing and Reading as Implemented in Third, Fourth and Fifth Grade Classes (ERIC ED294926, AERA 1988 paper)
notes: Two intermediate schools in Bay Shore, NY; teachers volunteered (62 percent of those invited) and all students in their classes took part; no student rule. The report calls its design pre-test post-test quasi-experimental, not a randomized trial, which a reviewer may want to check against Kraft's inclusion rule. Kraft n 441 is plausible for 24 classrooms. OCR is rough in places.

evidence_quote: The schools had been pre-selected by CPS using a series of school information sessions, initial interest applications, and site visits to assess staff’s ability and readiness to benefit from the program.
evidence_location: PDF p. 17, Chapter II.A Methods, footnote 2 (printed p. 6)
resolved_title: An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report. Final Report (Mathematica, April 2009)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: first page names Glazerman, McKie, and Carey (Mathematica Policy Research, April 27, 2009), the Chicago TAP year-one report Kraft cites. Sixteen CPS K-8 schools applied to become TAP schools, were chosen as finalists on staff readiness (application, site visits, faculty vote), and were then randomized 8 to treatment and 8 to delayed control; all students in those schools' test-score files form the sample. Schools that applied and were rated on readiness are volunteers, not selected on need (tie-breaker 6). No achievement or poverty criterion is stated. Kraft's n 3,501 was not located as a printed figure in the text.

evidence_quote: The lowest-ranking schools were designated as potential receiving schools that could benefit from the intervention, and the rest were potential sending schools.
evidence_location: PDF p. 31, Executive Summary, Study Sample (printed p. xxxi)
resolved_title: Transfer Incentives for High-Performing Teachers: Final Results from a Multisite Randomized Experiment (NCEE 2014-4003, November 2013)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: first page names Glazerman, Protik, Teh, Bruch, and Max (Mathematica, NCEE 2014-4003, November 2013), the Talent Transfer Initiative final report Kraft cites. Within each of 10 districts, schools were ranked by students' average prior achievement and the lowest-ranking schools became potential receiving schools; the 114 study schools were the receiving schools whose teaching teams with vacancies were randomized. Students are those taught by the randomized teams, with no student-level rule, so level is school. Districts were chosen for size and economic diversity (at least 40 elementary schools, 10 low-poverty and 15 high-poverty). Kraft's n 7,000 was not located as a printed figure in the text.
Retrieval status unresolved: no document, abstract, or WWC row exists for Cole 1992 (grade 4, n 268, math 0.57 and reading 0.51). No source, so no code.

evidence_quote: To address potential selection biases, the analyses exploit the random assignment that results from lottery-based admissions for a small set of schools, as well as value-added and fixed-effect estimators
resolved_title: Can Interdistrict Choice Boost Student Achievement? The Case of Connecticut's Interdistrict Magnet School Program
notes: Kraft grades 6-8 and n 494 point to the middle school lottery sample of magnet applicants; no achievement or demographic rule stated. Abstract says the program serves central city students but states no eligibility rule. WWC sample text adds only urban and suburban settings. The same WWC row is attached in error to study 202.

evidence_quote: The participants are 49 first-grade through fifth-grade classrooms from predominantly minority and poor contexts across the nation. Blocking by grade level within schools, the trial includes 27 classrooms receiving the OCR curricular materials and professional development and 22 business-as-usual control classrooms.
resolved_title: A Multisite Cluster Randomized Field Trial of Open Court Reading
notes: Whole classrooms randomized within 5 schools; no student rule. The abstract describes the sites as minority and poor but states no criterion for choosing them; if the full text shows sites were recruited for poverty, this becomes targeted_other at school level. Kraft n 1099 not checkable from the abstract. No WWC row.

evidence_quote: a district-level random assignment study fielded in over 500 schools within 59 school districts and seven states
resolved_title: A Multistate District-Level Cluster Randomized Trial of the Impact of Data-Driven Reform on Reading and Mathematics Achievement
notes: Districtwide reform with districts as the randomized unit and no student rule. The abstract gives no district recruitment criterion; a full-text check on whether CDDRE recruited districts for low performance or Title I status is needed, which would change the code to targeted at district level. Kraft n 31110 not checkable from the abstract. No WWC row.

evidence_quote: As an example, the CACE is estimated using data from a small, one-year field trial of vouchers in Charlotte, NC.
resolved_title: School Choice as a Latent Variable: Estimating the Complier Average Causal Effect of Vouchers in Charlotte
notes: Abstract describes the estimator, not the sample; it says only that treatment was a random offer of a voucher to applicants, so opt_in 1. Whether the voucher program had an income eligibility rule is not stated; if it did, this is targeted_other at student level. Kraft n 1143, grades 2-8. No WWC row.

evidence_quote: Both lottery and instrumental variable identification strategies suggest that the effects of attending an HCZ middle school are enough to close the black-white achievement gap in mathematics.
resolved_title: Are High-Quality Schools Enough to Increase Achievement Among the Poor? Evidence from the Harlem Children's Zone
notes: Lottery applicants to HCZ Promise Academy charter schools; no achievement or demographic rule stated in the abstract, though the title frames the population as poor. Kraft n 850, grades K-8, effects 0.04 and 0.12 likely the elementary or pooled lottery estimates. No WWC row.

evidence_quote: implementing a bundle of best practices from high-performing charter schools into low-performing, traditional public schools in Houston, Texas, using a school-level randomized field experiment and quasi-experimental comparisons
resolved_title: Injecting Charter School Best Practices into Traditional Public Schools: Evidence from Field Experiments
notes: Schools were chosen because they were low-performing (Houston Apollo 20); all students in treated schools served, so level school. Kraft grades K-5 and n 39464 match the elementary school-level experiment. Denver and Chicago results in the paper are not experimental. No WWC row.

evidence_quote: The study took place in 17 schools located in six TFA regions: Baltimore, Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles (Compton school district), the Mississippi Delta, and New Orleans.
resolved_title: Alternative routes to teaching: The impacts of Teach for America on student achievement and other outcomes
notes: Abstract states only that it is a randomized experiment on TFA teachers; the WWC setting text gives the 17 schools in TFA regions, where students were randomly assigned between TFA and other teachers. Sample is 95 percent FRPL by WWC, but no poverty rule for choosing schools is stated, so universal by the same logic as study 168. Kraft n 1800, grades 1-5.

evidence_quote: The district contains nine K-8 schools with a total of approximately 3,200 students. [...] program participation was made available to every K-8 classroom teacher, as well as reading and math interventionists.
resolved_title: Enhancing the Efficacy of Teacher Incentives Through Loss Aversion: A Field Experiment (NBER Working Paper 18237, July 2012)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: first page names Fryer, Levitt, List, and Sadoff (NBER w18237), the Chicago Heights teacher-incentive experiment that Fryer's reference 105 cites. All nine K-8 schools in the Chicago Heights, IL district took part; 150 of about 160 eligible teachers opted in and were randomized, and every student of those teachers is in the sample, so opt_in is 0 at the student level. The sample is 98 percent free or reduced-price lunch but nothing in the design selected on income. mixed_samples 1 because Kraft's study 297 folds four prekindergarten parental-incentive rows (n 257, Fryer, Levitt, and List 2015, NBER w21477) into the same study id; the two benchmark-cell rows (math, n 2,150, grades K-8) come from this trial, whose analysis samples are 2,144 and 2,347 students in the tables, and their PPVT label is a carry-over from the prek rows.
